newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 6.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company

-- GREAT WESTERN EXPANDS NORTH Great Western Holdings, which runs the Bristol to London rail line, yesterday won the North West Regional Railways franchise, extending its operations as far north as Carlisle. The company will receive more than one billion pounds stg of government subsidies to run the network over seven years.

-- GAS FURY AT BID BY REGULATOR TO SLIM TRANSCO British Gas yesterday reacted angrily to suggestions from industry regulator Clare Spottiswoode that the company's TransCo pipeline subsidiary could face further dismantling. The company denied an extensive breakup was underway and accused the regulator of causing unnecessary worry for employees and shareholders.

-- RJB BUYBACK PUSHES OUTLAY OVER 600 MILLION POUNDS RJB Mining, Britain's biggest coal producer, yesterday completed another share buyback worth 33 million pounds stg, pushing its outlay for debt repayment and share buyback over 600 million pounds over the last two years. The programme is designed to meet pre-flotation promises and prepare the company for tough bargaining over new coal contracts.

THE TIMES -- WALL STREET BANKS TO MERGE Morgan Stanley and Dean Witter, Discover, are to merge it was announced in New York yesterday. The merger will create the largest international investment bank in the world, with market capitalization of around 21 billion dollars US. John Mack, head of Morgan Stanley will be president of the combined company.

-- SCOTAM PUTS ITSELF UP FOR SALE AS PRU TOPS ABBEY BID Scottish Amicable has put itself up for sale following a bid of 1.9 billion pounds stg from Prudential which arrived just hours before Scottish Amicable was to have begun mailing a circular to its policyholders recommending that they accept the demutualisation and flotation plans put forward two weeks ago. The offer includes 400 million pounds stg in cash or Prudential shares to policyholders.

-- BT TO TAKE KEY STAKE IN DIGITAL VENTURE British Telecom is posed to be the largest shareholder in THe Interactive Serviced Company (Isco) which will help to finance the introduction of digital TV in Britain. The company is being formed to subsidise the retail price of the digital set top boxes to be ordered by BSkyB. Investors in Isco will share in the income generated by the interactive services made possible by the boxes.

-- GERMAN BACK ITALY TO HALT RUN ON LIRA Following reports that Italy's entry into the single currency could be delayed, the European Commission and Italian authorities, with the backing of the German government, moved to prevent a run on the lira. Early selling pressure was put on the Italian bonds and the lira after it was reported that Italy would not formally sign up for monetary union until 2000 or 2001.

-- CANARY WHARF PLANS 165 MILLION POUNDS RIVERSIDE SITE FOR APARTMENTS, HOTEL AND LEISURE The London Docklands Development project, Canary Wharf got a lift yesterday from the signing of an international deal to develop a site on the Thames. The development, a joint venture called Canary Wharf Riverside Development is expected to cost 165 million pounds stg and will not include any office space, consisting instead of luxury apartments, and hotel and leisure facilities.

-- HESELTINE IN ROW OVER PAYMASTER SELL-OFF A row is going on between the deputy Prime Minister, Michael Heseltine and senior Treasury officials who are trying to stop the pre-election privatisation of the Paymaster General's Office. Mr Heseltine wants the winning consortia, expected to be Capita, to be signed by February 14, allowing the agency to change hands by April 1 and preventing an incoming Labour government from stopping the sale.

-- CLARKE RATE HINT CONFUSES CITY Kenneth Clarke yesterday sent the pound soaring after his monetary meeting with Eddie George by appearing to hint he would raise interest rates in a lunchtime television interview. However, by the end of the day, it appeared most likely rates would not be changed, although the pound held its gains. Treasury said nothing could be read into the Chancellor's comments.

-- LLOYDS TO BUY OUT BRAZILIAN BANK Lloyds TSB is in talks to buy the consumer banking arm of its half-owned Brazilian associate, Banco Multiplic, a deal thought to be worth around 300 million pounds stg. Although Lloyds has been concentrating on its British operations and selling foreign assets recently, it has retained its Latin American presence.

-- AID FOR BELFAST PLANT OPPOSED European textiles manufacturers are to continue their battle against state aid for a Taiwanese project in Northern Ireland, which will see a plant built by the Hualon Corporation. The British Apparel and Textiles Confederation has decided to appeal a European Court ruling, which said that no rules were broken by the European Commission sanctioning 61 million pounds stg in subsidies for the plant. The plant may create up to 1,800 jobs in a deprived area north of Belfast.
